results.title: Beyond intent to treat (ITT): A complier average causal effect (CACE) estimation primer - ScienceDirect
results.content: Randomized control trials (RCTs) have long been the gold standard for allowing causal inferences to be made regarding the efficacy of a treatment under investigation, but traditional RCT data analysis perspectives do not take into account a common reality: imperfect participant compliance to treatment. Recent advances in both maximum likelihood parameter estimation and mixture modeling methodology have enabled treatment effects to be estimated, in the presence of less than ideal levels of participant compliance, via a Complier Average Causal Effect (CACE) structural equation mixture model. CACE model assumptions, specification, estimation, and interpretation will all be demonstrated with simulated data generated from a randomized controlled trial of cognitive-behavioral therapy for Juvenile Fibromyalgia. First, the simulated JFM RCT data were analyzed with a longitudinal SEM intent to treat (ITT) analysis, first with no covariates (an unconditional model), then with the inclusion of age, depression, pain severity and group (a conditional model). First, prior to removing the exclusion restriction and examining the change (if any) on the CACE treatment effect estimate as a result of adding additional covariates, we estimate a conditional *ITT* model to establish a comparison baseline. Results for the conditional ITT model illustrated in Fig. 7 showed that participants had an FDI score of 18.87 (*α*0 = 18.65, *p* < .001) at the start of the study, and control group. Taken together, results from all CACE analysis models suggest that a participant randomly assigned to the CBT treatment group, and found to be compliant with the treatment regimen, will tend to experience greater decreases in FDI scores over time versus a participant randomly assigned to the CBT treatment group but found to be non-compliant. ### Estimating psychological treatment effects from a randomized controlled trial with both non-compliance and loss to follow-up. * ### A task-shared, collaborative care psychosocial intervention for improving depressive symptomatology among older adults in a socioeconomically deprived area of Brazil (PROACTIVE): a pragmatic, two-arm, parallel-group, cluster-randomised controlled trial. We identified 24 primary care clinics in Guarulhos that were willing to participate, of which 20 were randomly allocated to either the control group (ten [50%] clusters) or to the intervention group (ten [50%] clusters).

results.title: Regression Discontinuity for Causal Effect Estimation in Epidemiology
results.content: Regression discontinuity analyses can generate estimates of the causal effects of an exposure when a continuously measured variable is used to assign the exposure to individuals based on a threshold rule. The regression discontinuity design can be thought of as an extension of instrumental variable analysis, in circumstances where an exogenous source of variation arises from a continuously measured random variable that at least partially assigns treatment or other exposure based on a threshold rule [9]. When the continuity assumption is met and there is exchangeability between patients above and below the threshold, the difference in the means at the threshold can be calculated, which can be interpreted as the average causal effect (ACE) in the population near the threshold in sharp regression discontinuity designs. Importantly, unlike in the randomized controlled trial, where the causal effect is identified for the entire patient population, in the regression discontinuity design, the causal effect is only identified at the threshold (unless additional assumptions are evoked) [20]. ### Instrumental Variable Methods for Estimating Complier Average Causal Effects in Regression Discontinuity Designs In the fuzzy regression discontinuity design, the effect of treatment among those who take treatment because of the threshold rule can be identified using instrumental variable methods [25]. Instrumental variable methods can be used within the regression discontinuity framework to identify the causal effect among the compliers, known as the complier average causal effect (CACE), where the instrument is eligibility for treatment (i.e., the threshold). Although, in the fuzzy regression discontinuity case, some individuals may not have taken treatment as assigned by the threshold, the RD-ITT is simply the population effect of the threshold. Regression discontinuity designs offer the opportunity to identify causal effects in the absence of randomized controlled trials by taking advantage of an exogenous source of variation in treatment assignment induced by a threshold rule. Perhaps most importantly, effects from regression discontinuity designs can only be generalized to individuals with assignment variable values that are close to the threshold. This study demonstrates that regression discontinuity designs can be used to re-analyze data from a trial to address concerns about non-compliance in the trial.** [DOI] [PubMed] * 11.•.Moscoe E, Bor J, Bärnighausen T.

results.title: Grand Rounds December 1, 2023: Guidelines for Design and Analysis of Stepped-Wedge Trials (James P. Hughes, PhD) - Rethinking Clinical Trials
results.content: # Grand Rounds December 1, 2023: Guidelines for Design and Analysis of Stepped-Wedge Trials (James P. Design, Analysis, Stepped-Wedge Trial. * There are several key design considerations for stepped-wedge design, including defining the estimand or what are you trying to estimate in the analysis, the key sources of variation, and how outcome data will be collected. Classic analyses of stepped-wedge trials assume that the effect of the treatment occurs instantaneously once the intervention is applied and that the effect of the intervention is constant over exposure time. Classic stepped-wedge analyses assume an instantaneous treatment effect. Researchers need to think very carefully about what is the possible exposure time curve and what is it the study is trying to estimate in the stepped-wedge trial? * An alternative approach to estimation in stepped-wedge trials compared to the standard immediate treatment approach is to use an exposure time indicator model, wherein researchers estimate a treatment effect for every exposure time. * Another issue to think about with stepped-wedge trials is potential sources of variation. For stepped-wedge trials there may be potential variation in treatment effect and variation in cluster means over time. * Key design recommendations for stepped-wedge trials: Don’t assume the intervention is immediate and constant (IT model) unless well-justified; if a transition period is planned, include data from the transition period; if the estimand is the effect at a point in time, maximize the number of observations at that exposure time; including more variance components in the power calculation reduces the possibility of an underpowered trial; and power calculations in SW trials can sometimes seem counterintuitive. * Key analysis recommendations for stepped-wedge trials: Fit flexible study time effect; avoid fitting IT model unless you are very confident that the intervention effect is immediate and constant; it is better to overfit than underfit random effects; use small sample correction if necessary. *-Most people have analyzed stepped-wedge designs with the immediate treatment model. *-In the stepped-wedge design there are no clusters that are always treated or never treated. If you had a cluster that was not treated it would probably improve your power but misses the point of the stepped-wedge design.

results.title: Stepped-Wedge Designs - Rethinking Clinical Trials
results.content: In stepped-wedge designs, the clusters are randomized into several groups or waves that define when the intervention will begin, and all clusters start the trial in the control condition. Stepped-wedge designs may also have the benefit of enabling researchers to record and incorporate into the analysis changes to the site or healthcare system that happen over time and have the potential to affect the study (Cook et al 2016). A further justification for stepped-wedge designs arises in the context of pragmatic trials where the interventions are presumed (often with little evidence) to be beneficial. As of 2022, all of the NIH Pragmatic Trials Collaboratory Trials that used a stepped-wedge design were granted a waiver of consent (Federico et al 2022). [A Policy-Relevant US Trauma Care System Pragmatic Trial for PTSD and Comorbidity (Trauma Survivors Outcomes and Support [TSOS])]() was a stepped-wedge, cluster randomized pragmatic clinical trial testing the delivery of a stepped collaborative care intervention vs usual care for injured patients with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and comorbid conditions. Several events during the TSOS trial led the research team to rethink the original stepped-wedge design, including a regulatory pause in the final period, when recruitment was only occurring in the intervention arm. Because of the staggered schedule of intervention rollout in the stepped-wedge design, this regulatory pause introduced a significant disruption to the trial’s implementation, and the researchers speculated that parallel randomization might have been better. The lesson learned at the end of the TSOS trial was that, regardless of whether the research team chooses stepped-wedge cluster randomization or parallel cluster randomization, site variability considerations favor individual-level randomization when possible. Dr. Liz Turner discusses arguments for and against using the stepped-wedge design when choosing the right cluster randomized trial in pragmatic research.
